chapters.title: Chapter 6: From One Asset to Two — An Introduction to Pairs-Based Reversion

lessons.title: Correlation Is Not Cointegration: A Quick Primer

children.text: Two stocks can move together almost every single day, rising on good market days, falling on bad ones, correlated at 0.85 or higher, and still be a terrible pairs trade. That sentence sounds like a contradiction until you separate two questions that look similar but are not: do these two stocks tend to move in the same direction, and does the gap between them stay within a bounded, predictable range. The first question is correlation. The second is cointegration. Only the second one actually tells you whether a pair is likely to mean-revert.

body.text: Correlation measures whether two series move in the same direction on average. Cointegration measures something stricter and more specific: whether the gap between two series, their spread or ratio, is itself a stationary, mean-reverting quantity, per the exact definition from Lesson 3. Two highly correlated stocks can still drift permanently apart. A pairs trade needs the second property, not the first.

children.text: How Correlated but Divergent Actually Looks

Take two hypothetical NSE-listed stocks in a related but not identical business. Both rise and fall together on most days, a daily return correlation of roughly 0.85, high enough to look like an obvious pairs candidate at first glance. But Stock X's business has been compounding earnings at 20% a year, while Stock Y's has been growing at closer to 5%. Both stocks feel the same market-wide and sector-wide days, which is what drives the high daily correlation, but their price ratio has climbed steadily from 1.0 five years ago to roughly 1.9 today, and shows no sign of coming back. A trader who shorted the ratio at 1.5, assuming it had to revert simply because the correlation looked strong, would have been fighting a genuine, structural growth gap the entire way, the exact structural growth case from Lesson 3, now happening to the relationship between two stocks instead of one stock's price.

body.title: Correlated but not cointegrated: two stocks, one diverging price ratio (illustrative)

body.text: Both lines rise together, dip together, and generally track each other's shape, which is exactly why the daily correlation looks strong. But the gap between them, Stock X's indexed value minus Stock Y's, keeps growing every single year. A high correlation between the wiggles is fully compatible with a steadily diverging level. That gap is what a pairs trade actually needs to be stable, not the day-to-day co-movement.

markDefs.definition: A formal statistical property where two individually non-stationary series (like two random-walk-like stock prices) combine, in some fixed proportion, into a new series that is itself stationary, per Lesson 3's definition.

children.text: when some specific combination of them, a price ratio, or more precisely a regression-based spread, is itself stationary, even though each stock's own price individually behaves like the non-stationary random walk from Lesson 3. This is a genuinely stricter requirement than correlation. Correlation is computed from daily returns and says nothing about the price levels drifting apart over years. Cointegration is a statement specifically about those levels, and whether their gap stays anchored.

body.title: Check whether a ratio looks bounded
body.prompt: A candidate pair's price ratio over six annual readings is: 0.95, 1.05, 0.88, 1.10, 0.90, 1.02. What is the range (maximum minus minimum) of this ratio over the period?
body.explanation: Maximum (1.10) minus minimum (0.88) = 0.22. A ratio oscillating within a fairly tight, bounded range like this, rather than climbing to new highs each year, is at least consistent with a mean-reverting relationship. This rough range check is not a substitute for formally testing cointegration, only a first-pass sanity check.

body.title: Which pair is the better candidate?
body.question: Pair A has a daily return correlation of 0.90, but its price ratio has climbed steadily from 1.0 to 3.5 over four years with no sign of reverting. Pair B has a lower daily return correlation of 0.65, but its price ratio has oscillated between 0.90 and 1.15 for the same four years. Which is the better candidate for a mean-reversion pairs trade?
options: Pair A, because higher correlation always makes a better pairs trade
Pair B, because its price ratio has stayed bounded, despite the lower correlation
Both are equally good, since correlation and cointegration always move together
Neither, because a pairs trade requires a correlation above 0.95
body.explanation: Pair A's high correlation describes strong day-to-day co-movement, but its steadily climbing ratio shows the relationship is not stationary, the structural growth case from Lesson 3. Pair B's lower correlation is less impressive on the surface, but its bounded, oscillating ratio is exactly the property a pairs trade actually depends on. Correlation and cointegration are different properties and can point in opposite directions.

body.text: This lesson is a primer, not the full test. Formally establishing cointegration requires the Engle-Granger method and the Augmented Dickey-Fuller test applied to the spread, exactly the machinery flagged as out of scope back in Lesson 3's collapsible section. A bounded-looking ratio over a handful of years, like the exercise above, is a useful eyeball check, not statistical proof. The full testing procedure, on real NSE and BSE pairs, is covered start to finish in Introduction to Statistical Arbitrage's own Chapter 3.

cards.definition: A statistical measure of whether two series' returns tend to move in the same direction, ranging from -1 to +1. Says nothing about whether their price levels stay anchored to each other over time.

A stricter property where some combination of two individually non-stationary price series, such as a ratio or regression-based spread, is itself stationary, the actual requirement for a pairs trade to be structurally sound.
The measured gap between two related securities, typically a price ratio or a regression-based difference, that a pairs trade is actually built to trade.

The standard formal statistical test for stationarity, and by extension for cointegration when applied to a spread between two securities. Outside this course's scope; covered fully in Introduction to Statistical Arbitrage.

points: Correlation measures whether two series' returns move together. Cointegration measures whether the gap between their price levels is itself stationary. These are different properties, and one can be strong while the other is absent.

Two highly correlated stocks can still see their price ratio drift permanently apart if their underlying growth rates differ, exactly the structural growth case from Lesson 3 applied to a relationship instead of a single stock.
A bounded, oscillating price ratio over time is a useful rough signal that a pair might be cointegrated, but it is not a substitute for formally testing it.

The formal test for cointegration, the Engle-Granger method and the Augmented Dickey-Fuller test on the spread, is explicitly outside this course's scope and is covered fully in Introduction to Statistical Arbitrage.
Lesson 3 closes this chapter by mapping out exactly where this course's coverage ends and where that deeper statistical arbitrage toolkit picks up.
